title: Bespoke Stainless Steel Fabrication for Commercial Kitchens
excerpt: How a clear specification brings together dimensions, equipment layout, materials and installation requirements for a commercial kitchen fabrication project.
content:
Bespoke fabrication allows stainless steel equipment to be designed around the space and working requirements of a commercial kitchen. Its value lies in resolving the details that a standard size cannot accommodate: a preparation surface between existing appliances, a sink arrangement suited to the workflow, or an extraction canopy aligned with the cooking equipment.

Midia M Metal manufactures and supplies commercial kitchen equipment. Its factory is in London. Its fabrication and installation work covers stainless steel kitchen equipment, ventilation systems, extraction canopies and wall cladding.

Define the function before the dimensions

The starting point is the work the equipment needs to support. A preparation table requires usable surface area and access from the appropriate sides. A sink unit needs a practical bowl arrangement and room for the items being washed. An extraction canopy belongs within a wider ventilation design.

Defining these requirements first makes the dimensions meaningful. It also identifies connections to adjacent equipment, water and waste services, walls or ductwork that need to appear in the specification.

Record the space accurately

Overall length, depth and height should be recorded alongside obstructions and connection points. Pipework, wall projections and nearby appliance doors can reduce the space available even when the main dimensions appear suitable.

A dimensioned plan establishes where the item sits. An elevation adds working heights and vertical clearances. Photographs provide context, while the drawings identify which dimensions have been checked and which remain provisional.

Specify the material and construction

A description such as “stainless steel table” leaves several decisions open. The material specification, surface finish, edge details, support arrangement and any openings need to be defined for the intended use.

Visible surfaces and connections to existing equipment deserve particular attention. A clear drawing can distinguish a finished edge from an edge that meets another unit, or identify where a joint needs to remain accessible after installation.

Consider installation during design

The completed item must reach its intended position. Doorways, corridors, stairs and turning space should be checked alongside the kitchen layout. An item that fits the room may still require a different assembly arrangement to pass through the building.

The agreed scope should identify what is being fabricated, what is being installed and which connections form part of the work. This gives everyone involved a consistent reference when preparing the site.

Keep one approved specification

Drawings, dimensions, material details and quantities should refer to the same revision. Recording changes in one approved specification helps prevent an earlier measurement or layout from being used during production. The resulting document describes the equipment as it is intended to be made and fitted.

title: Identifying Replacement Parts for Commercial Kitchen Equipment
excerpt: A practical guide to recording dimensions, fittings and product references when identifying replacement components for kitchen equipment.
content:
Identifying a replacement component starts with its relationship to the equipment. Two parts can look similar yet differ in fitting size, installed height or orientation. Recording those differences before ordering reduces the risk of selecting a component that cannot be fitted as intended.

For kitchen equipment components such as castors, feet and dividing bars, a product reference and a clear record of the existing arrangement are more useful than appearance alone.

Identify the equipment and the component

The equipment manufacturer, model and any component markings provide the first reference points. Where labels remain legible, the full reference should be recorded, including suffixes that may identify a particular size or version.

Photographs should show the complete item, the component in position and the connection between them. These views establish the context that is missing from a close-up of a detached part.

Separate overall dimensions from fitting dimensions

The overall size describes the space occupied by a component. Fitting dimensions describe how it connects. A castor, for example, has a wheel diameter and installed height as well as a mounting arrangement.

A useful measurement record identifies each dimension on a sketch. For a plate connection, that may include the plate size, hole diameter and hole spacing. A threaded fitting needs its actual thread specification; a similar-looking thread should not be treated as a match.

Use the original part as a reference

An existing component can help establish its shape and orientation, but wear or damage may have changed its dimensions. A bent section or enlarged fixing hole should be identified rather than copied without checking.

The equipment drawing or manufacturer's part information provides a useful comparison. If a matching component remains elsewhere on the same unit, its position should also be recorded, including any difference between left- and right-hand versions.

Check compatibility with the complete assembly

Fitting into the available space is one part of compatibility. The selected component also needs to suit the equipment's intended use and the manufacturer's specifications.

Replacing a foot or castor can affect the installed height of the unit and its relationship to neighbouring equipment. The condition of the mounting point matters too: a replacement component does not resolve a damaged connection.

Keep a component record

A concise record should contain the equipment reference, component reference, dimensions, quantity and supporting photographs. Keeping that information with the purchase record makes later replacements easier to identify and helps distinguish otherwise similar parts across a kitchen.

title: Planning Made-to-Measure Stainless Steel Worktops and Sink Units
excerpt: The layout decisions that shape a practical worktop, from preparation space and sink positions to service connections and installation access.
content:
A made-to-measure worktop should support the way a kitchen operates as well as fit its available space. Preparation, washing and plating each place different demands on the surface. Planning these activities together helps establish the arrangement before individual dimensions are fixed.

The most useful starting point is a plan of the working area showing the proposed surface, neighbouring equipment and the movement of staff between tasks.

Allocate usable working space

The full length of a worktop is not necessarily available for preparation. Sinks, draining areas and equipment placed on the surface all occupy part of it. Their positions should leave a practical area for the main task rather than divide the surface into awkward sections.

Depth and working height should be considered alongside reach and the surrounding layout. Where the new surface meets an existing table or unit, the junction and any difference in height need to be shown clearly.

Position sinks around the task

The number and dimensions of sink bowls should reflect what will be washed and how items move through the area. A bowl that accommodates the usual utensils may not accommodate the largest tray or container.

Water and waste connection positions belong on the drawing, together with the space required below the bowl. Locating the sink from the front edge and one defined end of the worktop makes its position easier to verify than a description such as “towards the left”.

Resolve the space underneath

Pipework, support positions and nearby equipment can compete for the same space below a worktop. The layout should show these elements together so that a support does not obstruct a connection or prevent access to an appliance.

Where equipment sits beneath the surface, its manufacturer's clearance requirements should form part of the design information. Available space should be measured around the complete equipment, including projections and connections.

Define edges and wall junctions

Front edges, exposed ends and the junction with the wall should be specified rather than left to assumption. Any upstand or opening needs a stated height, size and position.

The wall itself may not be straight or square. A plan should distinguish a nominal room dimension from the dimensions needed to achieve the intended fit, particularly when the worktop sits between two fixed surfaces.

Coordinate fabrication and fitting

Delivery access, the sequence of installation and the availability of service connections should be reviewed before the final drawing is approved. This is particularly relevant in an existing kitchen where equipment remains in place.

One current drawing should bring together the surface dimensions, sink layout, supports, openings and finish. It then provides a clear reference for both fabrication and installation.

title: Stainless Steel Kitchen Tables: Dimensions, Supports and Working Space
excerpt: How to plan a stainless steel kitchen table around its daily use, surrounding equipment, support layout and available access.
content:
A kitchen table occupies more space in use than its footprint suggests. Staff need room to work at it, equipment may project beyond its edges, and nearby doors or drawers need space to open. Assessing these relationships helps determine whether a table will work within the kitchen layout.

Start with the activity

A table used for food preparation has different layout priorities from one used for plating or supporting equipment. The working surface should accommodate the items used together during that task, with their usual positions considered from the outset.

A simple plan can show trays, containers or countertop equipment at their actual sizes. This gives a more useful picture of the available working area than the table dimensions alone.

Check access on every working side

The table's position should be assessed with the surrounding kitchen in use. Appliance doors, delivery routes and staff movement may all affect the space available around it.

A table placed against a wall will usually be approached differently from an island table. Its depth, orientation and relationship to adjacent surfaces should reflect that distinction. Where several people work at the same table, each task needs to be considered within the shared layout.

Plan the support arrangement

The support layout needs to suit the intended use and the equipment positioned on or beneath the table. A leg or cross member can obstruct an appliance even when there appears to be enough space between the outer edges.

Equipment dimensions and weight information should therefore accompany the layout. Any required load capacity belongs in the specification and should be confirmed for the finished table rather than inferred from its appearance.

Coordinate height and connections

The finished height includes the tabletop, frame and feet or castors. Where a table meets another surface, this complete dimension is the relevant one.

Adjustable feet and castors have different fitting requirements. A change between them should be assessed against the table design and intended use. It should not be treated as a simple change to the height shown on the drawing.

Check the route into the kitchen

Access measurements should include the narrowest doorway and any turn along the route. The table's length and depth both matter when moving it through confined space.

Confirming the working layout, support arrangement and access route together gives the final specification a practical basis. It also helps identify conflicts before the table is manufactured.

title: Selecting Castors and Feet for Commercial Kitchen Equipment
excerpt: The dimensions and product specifications to compare when selecting castors or feet, including mounting details, fitted height and intended use.
content:
Castors and equipment feet are often selected from a photograph of the existing part. A photograph is useful for identifying the general arrangement, but the product specification determines whether a replacement is compatible.

Keeping the fitting details separate from the overall dimensions makes it easier to compare products and identify which measurements still need confirmation.

Match the mounting arrangement

Castors may use a mounting plate, a stem or another specified fitting. Each arrangement requires different information. Plate dimensions and fixing-hole positions are relevant to a plate mounting, while a threaded stem needs a matching thread specification.

The manufacturer's drawing is the most reliable reference when one is available. Measurement notes should identify the points being measured so that a hole-centre dimension cannot be confused with an edge-to-edge dimension.

Compare the complete fitted height

Wheel diameter and total height describe different dimensions. The bracket and mounting arrangement contribute to the final height of the equipment as well as the wheel itself.

For replacement feet, the fitted height and adjustment range should be recorded where applicable. The aim is to compare the assembled equipment, not just the visible size of the detached component.

Use the specified load information

Product load ratings should be checked against the complete equipment and its use. The empty weight of a table or unit does not describe the weight of everything it may carry.

Manufacturer guidance should be used when selecting the required rating and arrangement. Assumptions based solely on appearance or on dividing a total weight by the number of wheels can miss relevant operating conditions.

Record movement and positioning requirements

The selection brief should explain whether the equipment stays in one position or moves between working areas. The route, floor surface, thresholds and available turning space provide useful context.

It should also identify the existing arrangement of fixed, swivel and braked castors. Any proposed change needs to be considered for the complete unit rather than as a series of unrelated replacements.

Build a clear comparison

A component schedule can place the existing and proposed product references alongside their fitting dimensions, total height and published specifications. Differences then become visible before an order is placed.

Manufacturer information illustrates why these details are listed separately: Blickle's castor specifications distinguish wheel dimensions, load capacity, fitting type and total height. These are separate checks even when two products appear similar.

title: Welded Joints in Stainless Steel Kitchen Fabrication
excerpt: Why joint position, preparation, assembly and finishing need to be considered together when specifying stainless steel kitchen equipment.
content:
Welding is one stage in the manufacture of stainless steel kitchen equipment. The finished result also depends on how the parts are designed, prepared, assembled and finished. A clear specification connects those stages instead of treating the visible weld as an isolated detail.

For a kitchen table, sink unit or extraction canopy, the position and purpose of each joint should be considered alongside the equipment's overall dimensions and intended use.

Define what the joint connects

A drawing should identify the components being joined and their relationship in the finished assembly. Material details, thicknesses and the joint arrangement provide the basis for deciding how the work will be carried out.

The intended use matters as well. A joint in a support assembly serves a different purpose from a joint between sheet-metal panels. Their requirements should be established within the design rather than inferred from a photograph of another item.

Prepare the joint as part of the process

Joint preparation includes the geometry of the connection and the condition of the surfaces to be joined. TWI's guidance on surface preparation for joining identifies both as essential parts of preparation.

This preparation takes place before the weld is made. It should not be confused with the finishing work carried out afterwards to achieve the specified surface appearance.

Plan assembly around the final dimensions

The fabrication drawing needs to describe the completed item, including its alignment with adjoining equipment. Dimensions that control a sink position, a support spacing or a duct connection should be easy to identify.

The assembly sequence also needs to leave access to the joints. Where one component would obstruct another, the order of work should be resolved during fabrication planning.

Agree the finish explicitly

A general instruction to provide a “neat finish” leaves room for different interpretations. The specification should identify which surfaces are visible, the appearance required and how the joined area relates to the surrounding material.

Where appearance is particularly important, an agreed reference sample can make the requirement clearer. The surface appearance and the acceptance requirements for the joint should both be addressed; one does not describe the other.

Review the complete item

The final review should consider the agreed dimensions, joint locations, connections and finish together. A table or canopy needs to fit its intended position as a complete assembly, with the relevant details matching the approved drawing.

Recording these requirements at the design stage gives fabrication and inspection a shared reference. It also makes later revisions easier to evaluate without relying on informal descriptions.

title: Planning Connections in Stainless Steel Kitchen Equipment
excerpt: How fixing positions, clearances and assembly access influence the fit of fabricated stainless steel equipment.
content:
Connections are easy to overlook when planning a piece of kitchen equipment. The main dimensions may be correct, yet an inaccessible fixing or an incorrectly positioned hole can prevent the assembly from fitting as intended.

Connection details should therefore be developed alongside the overall layout. They describe how the fabricated item relates to the surrounding equipment or structure, rather than simply adding holes to a completed design.

Describe both sides of the connection

The specification should identify what is being connected and the purpose of the connection. It may locate two components, secure a support or allow a section to be removed.

Drawings and photographs should show both mating surfaces. A detail of one component alone may omit the obstruction, offset or access restriction that determines the connection's final position.

Use a consistent measurement reference

Fixing positions are easier to verify when dimensions are taken from clearly identified reference edges. The drawing should state the hole sizes and centre positions, with the measurement units used consistently.

Offsets and changes in level should be shown in a side view where necessary. A plan view can describe the spacing accurately while concealing a difference in height between the two surfaces.

Leave room for assembly

A fixing requires more than enough space for the fastener itself. The installation sequence must allow access to position and secure the components with the appropriate tools.

This is especially relevant where equipment sits close to a wall or where adjacent items will be installed in sequence. A connection that is accessible in the workshop may be obstructed in its final position.

Identify removable components

If part of the assembly needs to be removed for access, that requirement should appear in the design information. The removal direction, clearance and access to the fixings need to be considered together.

The drawing should also distinguish fixed connections from adjustable positions. Leaving that distinction unresolved can lead to different assumptions during fabrication and fitting.

Coordinate the final details

Fixings, supporting surfaces and any required performance need to be specified for the actual installation. A similar-looking connection elsewhere does not establish the requirements for the new assembly.

Before production, the connection details should be checked against the latest layout and equipment information. Using the same drawing revision across the project helps keep hole positions, support locations and site measurements consistent.

title: What Determines the Cost of Bespoke Stainless Steel Fabrication?
excerpt: The specification details that influence fabrication cost and help make quotations for commercial kitchen equipment easier to compare.
content:
The cost of bespoke stainless steel equipment reflects more than its overall size. Two items with the same length and depth may require different materials, construction details and finishing work. A useful quotation describes those differences so that the price can be assessed against a defined scope.

For commercial kitchen projects, the clearest comparison starts with a common specification for the equipment and any associated installation.

Material and dimensions

The material specification, thickness and quantity form part of the manufacturing requirement. Overall dimensions establish the size, while the drawings define the separate pieces and how they fit together.

Material descriptions should be consistent across the quotation and drawings. A price based on an unspecified grade or thickness cannot be compared directly with one that includes a defined material requirement.

Construction and fabrication

Cut-outs, folds, joined sections and support arrangements all contribute to the work involved. A plain preparation surface differs from a sink unit with several openings and connections, even if both occupy the same floor area.

The relevant details should be shown in the specification. Otherwise, apparently similar quotations may be based on different assumptions about the finished item.

Surface finish and visible details

The required finish should identify the surfaces that remain visible and the treatment of edges and joined areas. Matching an existing installation may also require an agreed appearance reference.

Defining the finish before pricing allows it to be considered as part of the fabrication work. It also reduces uncertainty over what is included when the equipment is completed.

Quantity and repeatability

A requirement for several identical items should be distinguished from a requirement for similar items with different dimensions. Changes to sink positions, openings or supports can mean separate fabrication details.

An item schedule helps by giving each version its own reference and quantity. This makes the scope easier to price and provides a consistent record for checking the completed order.

Installation and project access

The quotation should state whether installation is included and identify the work covered. Access restrictions, the sequence of fitting and the relationship to existing equipment should be recorded where they affect the project.

Delivery arrangements, site work and any exclusions need to be clear enough to compare across proposals. They should not be assumed from the equipment description alone.

Compare the same revision

An estimate based on preliminary dimensions may change when the specification is developed. Keeping quotations linked to dated drawing revisions makes those changes easier to trace.

A meaningful comparison checks the material, dimensions, quantity, finish and installation scope together. The fabrication brief guide explains how to organise those details into a consistent project record.

title: Planning Commercial Kitchen Canopies and Ductwork
excerpt: How cooking equipment, canopy position, duct routes and installation access come together in a commercial kitchen ventilation brief.
content:
A commercial kitchen canopy should be planned as part of the ventilation system serving the cooking equipment. Its dimensions alone do not establish the requirements of the complete installation. The appliance arrangement, extraction provision, replacement air and duct route need to be considered together.

HSE's guidance on ventilation in catering kitchens identifies the cooking equipment and the effective capture of cooking fumes as central design considerations. Manufacturer information and a suitable system design provide the technical basis for the work.

Prepare an equipment schedule

The planning information should identify each appliance beneath the proposed canopy, including its model, dimensions, fuel type and position. Existing appliances and proposed additions should be shown separately so that the final cooking line is clear.

A layout drawing is particularly useful when several appliances sit together. It provides one reference for their positions and for the canopy's relationship to the surrounding walls and equipment.

Record the duct route

The proposed route should show where ductwork leaves the canopy, changes direction and reaches its intended discharge position. Ceiling levels, structural obstructions and other building services need to be included in the site information.

Photographs can document the visible route, while drawings identify dimensions and sections that need further checking. Unverified areas should be marked explicitly rather than treated as available space.

Include future access in the layout

HSE guidance highlights access to ductwork and removable grease filters as part of planning for cleaning. These access needs affect the layout of the installation and should be addressed before fabrication.

The design information should show how access is retained once nearby equipment and finishes are in place. An access point that is clear during fitting may become obstructed later in the project.

Define changes to an existing installation

When replacing a canopy or a section of ductwork, the brief should distinguish retained components from new work. Existing drawings, equipment references and the reason for the change help establish the extent of the project.

Site measurements should record the relevant interfaces, including connection positions and available space. This gives the replacement components a defined relationship to the installation around them.

Coordinate fabrication and installation

The approved information should bring together the equipment schedule, canopy dimensions, duct arrangement and installation scope. Any outstanding design details need to be resolved before they become assumptions in production.

Site access and the sequence of work should be planned alongside the kitchen programme. In an operating premises, the availability of the cooking area is a practical part of that planning.

title: Preparing a Clear Brief for Stainless Steel Fabrication
excerpt: A structured approach to recording dimensions, drawings, quantities and site information for a commercial kitchen fabrication project.
content:
A fabrication brief brings the essential project information into one place. It describes what is required, how the equipment will be used and which details are confirmed. This helps a fabricator assess the scope without relying on assumptions scattered across photographs, sketches and messages.

The brief does not need to begin as a complete technical drawing. It does need to distinguish known information from dimensions or design decisions that remain provisional.

Define the item and its purpose

Each item should have a clear description and reference. For a commercial kitchen project, that might be a stainless steel preparation table, sink unit, extraction canopy or wall cladding section.

The description should explain the intended use and its relationship to nearby equipment. A short account of the working arrangement is often more informative than a list of dimensions without context.

Organise dimensions on a drawing

A sketch should label the overall length, depth and height using consistent units. Sink positions, openings and connection points should be measured from identified reference edges.

Estimated dimensions should be marked as such. Where a measurement still needs checking, noting that uncertainty is more useful than presenting it as a production dimension.

Give photographs a clear purpose

A wide view establishes the location and surrounding equipment. Detail photographs record the connections, obstructions or existing surfaces that affect the fit.

Numbering photographs and referring to them on the sketch helps connect the views. For an existing installation, it is also useful to identify which equipment will remain and which elements belong to the proposed work.

Record materials, finishes and quantities

Known material and finish requirements should be included with the drawings. Undecided details should be listed for confirmation so they are not replaced by unrecorded assumptions.

An item schedule should distinguish identical items from different versions. Separate references are useful where units share an overall size but have different sink arrangements, openings or connection positions.

Describe the site requirements

Installation information should cover the location, access route and any restrictions on when the area is available. Doorways, stairs and fixed equipment may affect how a fabricated item reaches its position.

The brief should identify the installation work required and any connections being coordinated with other trades. A target programme can be recorded without treating an unconfirmed date as an agreed commitment.

Maintain a clear revision record

Drawings, photographs and written requirements should use consistent item references. When a detail changes, the current revision should replace the earlier instruction in the project record.

A clear brief allows the specification and quotation to develop from the same information. It also creates a useful reference for checking the equipment and installation against the agreed scope.
